newsitem.title: USA: Linenger walks off U.S. shuttle after months on Mir.
newsitem.headline: Linenger walks off U.S. shuttle after months on Mir.

text.p: U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger walked from the space shuttle Atlantis after returning to earth on Saturday from a four-month stay on Russia's troubled Mir space station, sources said.
The 42-year-old astronaut, who spent 132 days in space, walked from the shuttle, assisted by his flight surgeon, sources at the shuttle's landing strip told Reuters.
Atlantis swooped out of a partly cloudy sky and touched down at 9:27 a.m. EDT (1327 GMT) on the three-mile (5-km) runway at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre.
After the landing, Atlantis' commander, Charles Precourt, said Linenger was doing well.
"We're very happy to have had the opportunity to bring Jerry home," he said. "I can report he's up and about, feeling really great, in good spirits."
During its nine-day mission, the shuttle docked with Russia's Mir space station to collect Linenger and drop off his replacement, British-born U.S. astronaut Michael Foale.
"Feeling great and good to be home," Linenger told mission control soon after the landing. He rode back to Earth in a reclining chair to cushion him from the pull of gravity.
Spending months in weightlessness can cause bones to weaken and muscles to waste away. Astronauts often feel weak and woozy on their return to Earth.
Linenger, a medical doctor and Navy captain, had said he was determined to walk off the shuttle after its landing, despite NASA's preference for him to be carried off.
Officially, the space agency was reluctant to disclose how the astronaut disembarked from the shuttle.
"I wish the press wouldn't make this into some kind of athletic competition," NASA's shuttle-Mir programme director Frank Culbertson told a news conference earlier this week.
"I don't feel like it's healthy for our crew to feel like they're being identified as walking off or not walking off."
Only one of the four astronauts returning from long missions to Mir has admitted to being carried off.
During his stay on Mir, Linenger, who listed marathon running and ocean swimming among his hobbies, was to run daily for two hours on a treadmill to keep up his strength.
Although that exercise programme was disrupted by the problems aboard Mir, NASA did not expect any complications after Linenger's return to Earth.
A team of doctors and nurses was standing by in a special vehicle on the runway to examine the former Mir resident.
Space agency officials expected Linenger to regain his "Earth legs" within a few days and would make a full recovery of the debilitating effects of space travel within four months.
Linenger's four-month stay on Mir was marred by a serious fire, life support problems and a near collision with an unmanned cargo craft.
The highlight of the mission came in April when Linenger and his Russian commander, Vasily Tsibliev, stepped outside on a spacewalk, the first by an American from Mir.
Linenger's 132-day stay in space was the second-longest mission for an American astronaut. Shannon Lucid set the U.S. record with a 188-day stay on Mir in 1996.
Linenger said he expected to feel "pure elation" when he was reunited with his 18-month old son, John, and his wife, Kathryn, who is eight-months pregnant with their second child.
Space agency chief Daniel Goldin brought the astronaut an arrangement of yellow tulips to pass on to his wife and a present for his son.
"He couldn't go out to a store in space," Goldin said.
Atlantis, which blasted off on May 15, spent five days docked at the Russian orbital outpost.
In addition to swapping astronauts, the shuttle carried to Mir two tonnes of much-needed supplies and equipment, including an oxygen generator and gear to plug cooling system leaks.
Foale, the fifth U.S. astronaut to live and work on Mir, is to return to Earth in September.

Atlantis' touchdown was delayed 90 minutes by cloudy skies at the Florida spaceport. Flight controllers in Houston watched the weather until the last minute before giving the shuttle permission to land.
